Rate consultants (Raftelis, FCS, Hazen) do fee-based apparent-loss reviews at system level with sampling, not ranked account-level dollars with test certificates. EagleView and imagery vendors solve parcels, not meters. We drop ghost parcels as the headline and avoid the contingency-contract and back-billing exposures the parent's research flagged.

mutants.title: Revenue-Integrity Diligence for Water System Acquirers
mutants.one_liner: The buyer of a small or mid-size water system pays for a 10-day, account-level scan of the target's billing, meters and parcels. It prices hidden revenue and revenue-quality risk before signing, then a success fee on prospectively recovered revenue funds the first-100-days fix.
mutants.customer: Corporate development and integration leads at serial acquirers of municipal and small private water and wastewater systems. These are the acquisition teams of investor-owned utilities, PE- and infrastructure-fund-backed water platforms, contract operators bidding O&M or concession deals with revenue share, and regional authorities absorbing failing systems. Deal size is systems with 3k-60k connections.
mutants.problem: Buyers price municipal systems on reported revenue and customer counts. Their diligence covers engineering condition, financial audit and legal. Nobody tests account-level billing integrity beyond sampling a few bills. Sellers cannot fix leakage themselves: correcting a meter class, adding unbilled connections or raising a billing floor is politically radioactive for a council, and back-billing is legally capped. So the leakage stays buried until after close. The buyer then discovers it over years, after the price is set, so the buyer neither benefits from knowing it at pricing time nor budgets capex against it. The same blind spot hides negative surprises: estimated reads, stopped meters, dead accounts and customer counts that overstate the base.
mutants.solution: Ask the seller's data room for a standard extract: account list, 24-36 months of consumption, meter inventory, rate class and tariff, receivables aging. Join it to the assessor roll, building footprints, permits and public filings. Produce a Revenue Integrity Report in 10 days: (1) a parcels-with-structures versus billed-connections gap by service area; (2) a large-meter low-flow fingerprint ranking accounts by expected annual dollars; (3) read-quality and zero-read audit (estimated reads, stopped meters); (4) misclassified rate class or meter size; (5) a downside adjustment to the revenue baseline; (6) a 100-day plan with a prospective-only fix, a meter test and replacement list, and a price-adjustment memo for negotiations. After close, execute the plan with the buyer's CIS and the field-test subcontractor, and later normalize billing data across the buyer's whole portfolio.
mutants.why_now: PFAS, lead-line and aging-pipe capex plus affordability politics push small municipal owners toward selling or regionalizing. Serial acquirers and infrastructure funds are actively rolling up water systems. Fair-market-value sale statutes (for example Pennsylvania's Act 12) have made municipal sales a repeatable process. Diligence windows are short (30-60 days of exclusivity), which fits a 10-day data product. Open footprint data, interval data and LLM-assisted cleaning of messy municipal billing exports make a 10-day turnaround possible for two people.
mutants.revenue_model: Fixed diligence fee of $35-75k per target, paid from the deal budget and owed even if the buyer walks. Success fee of 15-20% of verified incremental billed revenue over 24 months post-close (prospective only, verifiable in the buyer's own CIS). Optional 100-day revenue plan retainer of $15k a month. Then a portfolio SaaS tier for serial acquirers: $3-6k per system per year for cross-system revenue-integrity monitoring. Bottom-up assumption: 30-60 diligence engagements a year at about $50k is $1.5-3M of revenue for a small team.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The same $1 of recurring recovered revenue is worth about $1 a year in a city budget, but roughly 8-15x that to an acquirer valuing the system on earnings, and the buyer can bill correctly on day one. Change of ownership is the only moment when meter-class and connection corrections carry no council optics and no back-billing exposure. Payer and problem-owner are misaligned in the parent idea (the city pays for a fight it does not want). Moving the buyer of the utility into the payer seat removes procurement, contingency-ban and optics risk in one step. It also works as an option-free downside screen, which a buyer values on every deal, not only the rich ones.
mutants.first_30_days: Build a list of about 40 acquirers from state PUC acquisition dockets, fair-market-value sale filings and municipal sale RFPs. Pick three live or recently announced sale processes. Run a free public-data teaser for each: assessor parcels with structures inside the service area versus service connections in SDWIS and PUC filings, plus the top customers in the seller's annual financial report. Send two-page teasers to corporate development heads. Recruit one advisor, either ex-corporate development at a water utility platform or a water-M&A deal lawyer, for warm intros. Offer a half-price pilot diligence ($15-20k) on one live deal with a data-room extract. Confirm buyers' NDAs allow use of aggregated, anonymized yield data.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Itron, Badger, Master Meter and Metron sell hardware plus analytics to utilities that already own the system, and they do nothing at deal time. Ameresco-style ESCOs sell projects after ownership is settled. Rate and valuation consultancies (Raftelis, FCS, Hazen and peers) are often on the seller side or the municipality's side, and they use sampled tests rather than account-level joins, which makes a buyer-side, conflict-free diligence product counter-positioned against them. Big-4 and engineering diligence cover financial and asset condition, not billing integrity. The AWWA audit is system-level and free but names no accounts. EagleView and BlueConduit sell parcel data or a lead inventory, not a buyer-paid revenue-quality report. There is no public procurement and no contingency-contract exposure, because the payer is a private acquirer.

mutants.title: Big-Meter Replacement Fund, Repaid by Verified Uplift
mutants.one_liner: A meter-brand-neutral fund buys, installs and owns a utility's worst large meters at zero upfront cost. The utility repays 70% of measured incremental revenue for up to 5 years, with an open verification protocol that makes it an underwritable asset class.
mutants.customer: Utilities with 5k-100k connections that know their big meters are old but have no capex or staff. That is most utilities carrying PFAS and lead-line programs. The wedge buyer is a city or district finance director who can sign a no-cost, contingent-payment services contract under their small-purchase limit. Later, infrastructure lenders and the SRF or muni-lease programs that co-finance the fund.
mutants.problem: Replacing a large meter is a financing problem, not an information problem. A top-quartile large meter (3-10 inch) costs about $5-25k installed and can recover $6-15k a year in missed water and sewer revenue, which is a payback of about 1-2 years. Yet it stays unfunded. The benefit lands in the revenue line that nobody budgets as upside, while the cost hits scarce capex competing with lead lines and PFAS treatment. Council needs a procurement, an appropriation and a crew. An audit like the sharpened version tells them what to fix, but leaves them to fund and execute it. ESCOs bundle it into large projects with the vendor's own hardware, and meter vendors finance only their own meters.
mutants.solution: Underwrite: the screen ranks candidate meters by expected uplift and only meters with payback under about 2 years enter the fund. Verify: an open measurement and verification protocol (pre-swap on-site accuracy test at three flow rates, post-swap test, then 12 months of billing versus matched peer accounts) in the style of IPMVP for energy. Fund: the fund buys meters through distributors at volume and pays independent plumbers and a test subcontractor for the swap. Repay: the utility pays a metering-service fee of 70% of verified incremental revenue per meter, for up to 60 months or until 1.8x of capital is returned, never more, then owns the meter. Payments are contingent, not debt, and recovery is prospective, so no back-billing. Every swap adds a before-and-after label to the yield model, which lowers the cost of capital. Later, pool contracts and sell them to infrastructure debt or bank warehouse lines.
mutants.why_now: Revenue-backed, measured-savings financing has already worked for solar PPAs and energy performance contracts once a standard M&V existed. Water meters have none. Utilities are capital-starved by PFAS and lead-line mandates and need off-balance-sheet fixes. AMI interval data makes before-and-after verification cheap enough to sell to lenders. Data engineering means a small team can build the underwriting model, and distributors are eager to move meter volume.
mutants.revenue_model: Return on deployed capital: assumed 25-30% net unlevered (about $9k average installed cost, about $6k a year of measured uplift, 70% share, 2-2.5x lifetime multiple, less yield and dispute losses). Fees: 3-5% origination and a verification fee per meter. Later: a warehouse line then securitization of the contract pool. Data licensing of the accuracy-by-model-and-age dataset to lenders, consultants and vendors. Start-up capital: a $250-400k first pilot from angels or a revenue-based lender, plus extended payment terms from a meter distributor.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: An accurate large meter is a small, measurable cash-producing asset with almost no credit risk, because its yield, not the city's credit, pays it back. What is missing is a trusted way to measure the yield. Whoever writes and owns the verification protocol and holds the labeled before-and-after data has a standard-setter's position and a compounding cost-of-capital advantage: each verified swap makes the next loan cheaper. Meter distributors are suppliers and floor-plan lenders here, not enemies, because the fund is a volume buyer that creates demand they cannot create.
mutants.first_30_days: Write v0.1 of the verification protocol as a 2-page public document and get two reviewers: a water-loss practitioner and a municipal attorney (to review the contingent service-contract form and the state's non-appropriation rules). Get 90-180 day terms from two distributors on 25 large meters and a rate for a test-rig subcontractor. Run free top-100 scans for 6 utilities of 10-40k connections and pick the one with the best yield and a cooperative finance director. Propose a no-cost 25-meter pilot with 70% of verified uplift for 60 months. Line up the first $250-400k. Aim to have the pilot contract on a council agenda inside 90 days.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Itron, Badger, Master Meter and Metron sell meters and analytics, and financing tied to their own hardware would cannibalize their revenue models. They also cannot credibly say the installed base under-registers. Ameresco and other ESCOs bundle AMI and big-scope projects with slow cycles and vendor hardware, and they typically pursue larger projects, so our small verified-uplift tickets sit below their minimums (unverified). Bank lease-purchase programs and SRF loans make the utility carry the yield risk and need appropriation and procurement, whereas ours are contingent payments. EagleView and BlueConduit are data vendors with no capital. Consultancies advise but do not fund. AWWA's free audit is system-level and identifies no accounts. The independent M&V protocol and the private labeled dataset are the moat.

mutants.title: Materials Capture Ratio: Pay-on-Lift for Flat-Rate Shops
mutants.one_liner: Measure what share of the parts a residential plumbing or HVAC shop buys actually reaches a customer invoice, coach the leak out tech by tech and job type, and charge 25% of the measured lift over a frozen baseline.
mutants.customer: Owner and office manager of residential plumbing and HVAC service-and-replacement shops with 8-25 trucks and $2-8M revenue. They run flat-rate pricing on Housecall Pro, FieldEdge or Jobber (or ServiceTitan without Procurement/AP) plus QuickBooks Online, and techs pull from truck stock restocked on account at Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply or a local house. First job types are water heater replacement and condenser/air-handler swaps, where the standard install kit is well defined (expansion tank, flex connectors, T&P valve, discharge pipe, gas flex, line set, disconnect, pad, whip). Reached through PHCC chapters and owner masterminds.
mutants.problem: The parent idea has three weak spots. (1) Retroactive found money is mostly uncollectible. A homeowner will not pay a $40 parts add-on six months after a completed job, so an audit that reports history overpromises. Real value is capturing correctly from now on. (2) Contingency on 'newly captured revenue' cannot be attributed, so owners will dispute the fee. (3) Ticket-to-job matching from emailed PDFs is messy because counter tickets carry a typed job name at best, and these shops have no PO-per-job discipline for a 3-way match. Meanwhile the recurring leak is real and habitual. Techs bill labor from the flat-rate book and forget the $6 valve, the wax ring or the whip, and nobody sees it because the two ledgers (supply-house spend and customer invoices) are never divided into each other.
mutants.solution: Lead with one owner-legible KPI, the Materials Capture Ratio (MCR): materials billed at cost divided by materials purchased at cost, by month, tech, job type and supplier. It is computed from two exports and needs no invoice-by-invoice matching. Read-only OAuth into QuickBooks Online pulls supply-house bills and restock POs. A CSV or API export from the field-service software supplies the invoice material lines. Day one output is 'of every $100 of parts you buy, you bill $X', per tech. Then learn the shop's own kit per top-10 flat-rate job type by parsing a sample of supply-house lines with an LLM, and each week send the office manager a missing-parts list: closed jobs whose invoice lacks items the kit says were bought, with the pricebook item ready to add, plus which are still rebillable (open T&M, commercial, home-warranty and maintenance-agreement jobs). Add a pre-invoice nudge in the tech's flow later. Supplier-side price drift, unclaimed return credits and repricing files are a free add-on from the same data, not the headline. Contract: freeze a 6-month baseline MCR from the export, then charge 25% of (MCR lift x purchases x the shop's own average materials markup) for 12 months, with the shop's accountant signing the baseline once. It converts to a $199-499 per month subscription that includes the peer MCR benchmark.
mutants.why_now: Tariff-driven list-price moves mean flat-rate pricebooks go stale in a quarter, so owners are already asking where margin went. LLMs make it cheap to learn a shop's per-job kit from messy supplier lines. QuickBooks Online and the field-service platforms now expose APIs and exports, so onboarding takes minutes rather than a consulting project. The 2025 copper, steel and aluminum tariff regime, per the parent's research, made materials cost the most volatile line in a service shop's P&L.
mutants.revenue_model: Year one is a pay-on-lift fee of 25% of measured incremental materials revenue over the frozen baseline (no lift, no fee), which pairs a low-risk sale with a clean way to dispute-proof attribution. Then a $199-499 per month monitoring and benchmark subscription. Illustration: a $4M shop that lifts capture by 1-2% of revenue recovers $40-80K a year and we earn $10-20K in year one. If the median shop's gap is under 0.5% of revenue, the hypothesis is falsified within 30 days.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the found dollars. It is the rate of capture, a ratio you can compute from two exports without matching one ticket to one job, which sidesteps the parsing problem and the retroactive-billing problem together. Pegging the fee to a pre-agreed baseline ratio makes the contingency indisputable, which the parent lacked. Level is not the point, since warranty parts, callbacks and inventory build legitimately lower MCR. What matters is the delta and the spread between techs on the same job type, and that spread turns a vague back-office audit into a coaching scoreboard the owner can act on Monday morning. Pooled over many shops, the per-job-type kit and the MCR distribution become the cornered data asset.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-7: recruit 8 shops from PHCC chapters and owner masterminds on Housecall Pro, Jobber or FieldEdge with QuickBooks Online. Get read-only QBO access and one invoice-line export each. Days 7-10: compute MCR by tech and by job type in a notebook and deliver a one-page 'you buy $100, bill $X' result within 48 hours of data. Days 10-20: learn the water-heater and condenser-swap kits from supply-house lines, and produce the missing-parts list for the last 60 days as a coaching artifact, not a bill. Day 14-30: ask each shop to sign a 12-month pay-on-lift agreement with the baseline frozen from the export, and start the weekly missing-parts email. Kill test: if the median gap between the top-quartile and bottom-quartile tech MCR is under 3 points, or shops will not accept the baseline, drop or pivot. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so also manually check r/HVAC, r/Plumbing and Crunchbase for small funded entrants before spending on building.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: It drops the supplier-invoice-audit-software pitch that collides with ServiceTitan AP, Kojo and BuildOps, all of which police what the shop pays suppliers via PO and receipt 3-way matching. It sells the customer-side billing leak they do not market, and it works without POs, receipts or job-level ticket matching, so it fits Housecall Pro, Jobber and FieldEdge shops and ServiceTitan shops that never turned on Procurement/AP, the segment the parent's research called uncontested. Kojo and BuildOps are built for larger commercial contractors with PO discipline, Ramp is a horizontal AP tool, and MarginEdge serves restaurants. No one offers an outcome-priced, done-for-you service, and the supplier-side price-drift findings are a bundled extra rather than a head-on feature fight. Platform risk is limited because a field-service vendor that earns on payments and pricebooks has little reason to audit an owner's tech-by-tech compliance and publish peer benchmarks.

mutants.title: Materials-Leakage Diligence for Trade-Shop Acquirers
mutants.one_liner: Sell search-fund, independent-sponsor and roll-up buyers of plumbing/HVAC shops a five-day report that reconciles the target's supplier spend to its customer invoices, sizes the fixable leak as EBITDA, and sets the baseline for a post-close capture program.
mutants.customer: Search-fund CEOs, independent sponsors and PE platform add-on teams buying residential plumbing, HVAC and electrical shops with $2-15M revenue, plus the SBA and ETA lenders and small quality-of-earnings shops that can white-label it. They are repeat or well-networked buyers who already spend on diligence and want a differentiated, quantified edge.
mutants.problem: Lower-middle-market trade deals are underwritten from a QuickBooks P&L and a seller-prepared add-back schedule. Gross margin looks acceptable or off, but the buyer cannot tell whether materials margin is real, leaking through unbilled truck-stock parts, or dragged by supplier price drift and stale pricebooks. Buyers discover the leak after closing, when the owner-operator's habits are theirs to fix. The parent idea has the same structural flaws sold to shop owners: owners feel a $10K fee is expensive and resist behavior change, and recoveries are hard to attribute. Generic accounting-firm quality-of-earnings work is done at general-ledger level, as far as I can tell, and rarely reconciles supplier spend to customer invoice lines, especially for shops this small.
mutants.solution: A fixed-scope, five-business-day 'Materials Truth Report' run in confirmatory diligence. The seller shares read-only QuickBooks and a field-service invoice export through the data room. The report gives (1) 24 months of Materials Capture Ratio (materials billed at cost divided by materials purchased) by job type, tech and supplier, compared with a pooled peer range; (2) supplier price position, meaning multiplier drift, surcharges and unclaimed credits versus the shop's own history; (3) truck-stock and inventory reasonableness; (4) a normalized gross-margin range for EBITDA underwriting; and (5) a 100-day capture plan with dollar values by lever (kit-based pricebook fixes, tech coaching, repricing file, supplier renegotiation). After closing, the buyer keeps the shop on a capture program measured against the diligence baseline, which was agreed pre-close and so cannot be disputed. Roll-ups get a portfolio dashboard comparing all acquired shops.
mutants.why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings since 2025 made materials margin the least trustworthy line in a trade shop's books, and buyers have been burned. HVAC and plumbing are consistently among the most-targeted sectors for search funds, independent sponsors and PE add-ons, so diligence differentiation is now a buyer priority. LLM parsing of supplier lines lets a two-person team deliver in a week what would otherwise be weeks of associate time. Field-service and accounting platforms expose exports, so a seller can share data in minutes.
mutants.revenue_model: Buyer pays $7,500 per target ($2,500 at engagement, $5,000 at close, or the full fee if delivered with the deal dead, negotiable). Post-close, either 20% of measured uplift over the diligence baseline for 12 months, or $500 per shop per month for roll-up portfolio monitoring. White-label to QoE boutiques and lenders at $3,000 wholesale per report. Value logic for the buyer: on a $6M shop, one point of revenue is $60K of EBITDA, worth roughly $200-350K of purchase price at 3.5-6x, so a $7.5K report is a rounding error next to the price adjustment or the 100-day plan value it produces.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Changing the payer fixes three flaws at once. Authority: a new owner can change technician compensation, pricebook and process on day one, while an incumbent owner-operator rarely will. Attribution: the diligence baseline is a pre-agreed, third-party measurement, so uplift fees are not disputable. Willingness to pay: to a buyer the leak is enterprise value, not annual cash, so it justifies fees that would scare a shop owner. It also reverses the sales problem. Instead of selling to thousands of busy owners, you sell repeatedly to a few hundred networked buyers who talk to each other in search-fund and independent-sponsor communities, and each diligence adds a shop to the pooled benchmark without a per-shop sales effort. Roll-ups are the natural repeat customer and the natural distribution channel for the capture program.
mutants.first_30_days: Build a list of 40 search-fund and independent-sponsor buyers with live trade-shop deals (newsletters, ETA communities, LinkedIn, broker teasers). Offer the report free on one live deal in return for permission to cite anonymized findings. Aim for 3 live deals by day 30, with delivery within 5 business days of data access. In parallel, talk to two small QoE shops about white-labeling. Convert the first paid engagement on the next deal at $7,500. Position it as confirmatory diligence after an LOI, since sellers resist sharing invoice lines pre-LOI. Track whether the median target shows a capture gap worth more than $100K of EBITDA-equivalent, which tells you if buyers will keep paying. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so first check for any existing tech-enabled trade diligence vendors.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: ServiceTitan AP, Kojo, BuildOps and Ramp all sell operating software to the shop, which must adopt it, keep POs and receipts clean, and run it weekly. This is a one-time attested analysis sold to the buyer, produced from an export of whatever field-service system and QuickBooks the target already uses, so nothing has to be adopted and it works on Housecall Pro, Jobber, FieldEdge and ServiceTitan targets alike. ServiceTitan's statement and credit tools overlap only on the supplier-side piece, which here is a secondary section, not the product. No platform vendor has any incentive to produce third-party diligence on a shop being sold to a competitor, and MarginEdge-style tools are restaurant-only. The buyer relationship also gives a natural route into the parent's capture program after close without selling to the shop from scratch.

mutants.title: A Price Reporting Agency for Trade Materials
mutants.one_liner: Turn pooled supply-house invoices into contract-grade, SKU-level price evidence for the trades, starting with cost-change certificates that win price-adjustment change orders and ending as the index that escalation clauses and price-lock guarantees reference.
mutants.customer: First: plumbing, HVAC and electrical subcontractors with $3-30M revenue that carry fixed-price bids, multi-month jobs and maintenance agreements and eat cost changes between bid and buy. End state: the counterparties who write and argue escalation clauses, meaning general contractors, property owners and managers, municipal procurement, insurers, home-warranty programs, lenders, and the manufacturers and distributors who want realized-price data.
mutants.problem: Price adjustment requests are argued with anecdotes. A sub says copper fittings and water heaters are up 15-20% since the bid, and the GC or owner asks for proof. Broad public benchmarks (producer price indices and estimating books) are category-level and lag what contractors actually pay by SKU at their contractor multiplier in their region, and supplier price letters flow to contractors with a long lag, as the parent's tariff research noted (50% Section 232 copper duty from August 1, 2025). Subs either absorb the difference on fixed-price work or lose weeks assembling invoices by hand. There is no independent, contract-grade reference that both sides of a contract accept, as far as the parent's research and I could find. Parent idea limit: a per-shop audit keeps price data private and never becomes anything a counterparty trusts.
mutants.solution: Step 1 (months 0-6) sells a Cost-Change Certificate. For a sub with a fixed-price contract or bid, we parse its own supplier invoices and quotes into a SKU-normalized evidence pack: cost at the bid date versus cost at purchase, supplier price-letter references, invoice copies, and the escalation amount calculated by the contract's own formula, reviewed by the shop's accountant. It needs no network on day one, only one shop's invoices. Step 2: every certificate is paid partly in data, since the shop opts in to contribute its anonymized line items to the pool and in exchange gets a free alert feed ('your PEX-A fitting cost is 9% above the regional median'). Step 3 (months 6-18): publish weekly transaction-based indices by category and region, with a 30-day lag, minimum-contributor thresholds, no supplier or shop names, to stay clear of price-signaling and confidentiality problems. Owners, GCs and municipalities start writing 'adjusted per [Index] Copper Fittings, Region' into contracts and pay for verified access. Step 4 (months 18-36): price-lock guarantees for quoted jobs, underwritten off the index through an MGA or reinsurer partner, where shops pay a small premium on covered materials and we carry the basis risk we understand better than anyone.
mutants.why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings made price adjustment a routine dispute in 2025-26, and owners and GCs are rewriting price-adjustment language. The barrier to a transaction index was always normalizing hundreds of supplier catalog and invoice formats into comparable SKUs, and LLMs just made that cheap. Field-service and accounting systems make invoice ingestion easy. The volatility also means the certificate solves a painful, dated, dollar-denominated problem today, not a theoretical data project.
mutants.revenue_model: Certificates at $250-400 each, or 15-20% of the escalation actually approved (better alignment on big claims). Then index subscriptions of $500-2,000 per month for GCs, owners, insurers and municipal buyers who want verified reference access, with data licensing to manufacturers and distributors for realized-price and sell-through data. Later underwriting margin on price-lock guarantees, priced at roughly 1.5-3% of covered materials. Example: a sub with a $400K contract that is 30% materials and 8% higher-cost has a $9,600 claim, and a 20% success fee on half of that approved is about $1,000 per contract.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: In commodity markets the durable business is not the data feed but being the named reference in contracts, which is why price reporting agencies for metals and lumber have switching costs no feed provider has. The way in is not a dashboard. It is a document that ends an argument, sold to the party who is losing money now. The certificate requires no network on day one, and the network appears as a byproduct because every certificate adds contributed data. It is also a position platform vendors and supply houses structurally cannot take. ServiceTitan and Kojo depend on supplier integrations such as Ferguson and Hajoca, and publishing cross-customer price data pits those partners against their users, while a supply house cannot publish its own multipliers.
mutants.first_30_days: Recruit 5 light-commercial mechanical and plumbing subs with open fixed-price contracts where costs have risen since bid (owner peer groups, PHCC and ACCA chapters). Build the SKU normalizer for the top 200 SKUs (copper tube and fittings, PEX, PVC, water heaters, gas flex) across Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply, Home Depot Pro and local-house formats. Produce 5 certificates within 2 weeks and record how each GC or owner responds, since approval rate and dollars approved are the key learning. Sign 3 shops to the contingency version. Publish a free monthly 'copper fittings' note from the first shops' data (with disclosure) to seed the brand. Have an attorney review the contribution agreement and the aggregation and lag rules before publishing anything pooled. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so verify that no existing indices or claim-documentation vendors serve this niche.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: ServiceTitan AP, Kojo's Sourcing Grid, BuildOps, Ramp and MarginEdge all keep price data private per customer to help that customer buy or pay better. None produces a third-party-verifiable, cross-shop reference that a counterparty accepts, and none sells to GCs, owners, insurers or municipalities. Platform vendors will not publish it because it turns their supplier integration partners (Ferguson is a named ServiceTitan integration) into adversaries. Kojo focuses on larger commercial contractors' purchasing, while this works from the invoices of any shop regardless of field-service software, so Housecall Pro, Jobber and FieldEdge shops are included without any adoption. It also moves the monetization away from the crowded supplier-invoice audit toward evidence and a standard, where the incumbents have no product.

mutants.title: Yen Gap Audit for Legacy Seven Owners
mutants.one_liner: A flat-fee LINE audit that takes HQ's own AI order proposal as the baseline and shows Kansai multi-store Seven-Eleven owners, per item and delivery slot, the yen gap between what HQ suggests and what their own 15/85 contract says they should order.
mutants.customer: Owner-operators (individuals or small corporations) running 3 to 10 legacy-contract Seven-Eleven stores in Osaka, Kyoto and Hyogo, who have a contract renewal or a new-store offer within 24 months. Legacy stores are the narrow wedge because Seven's new contract (50/50 disposal share, effective autumn 2027) applies only to newly opened stores with no conversion planned, so the 15/85 asymmetry persists on existing stores for years. Multi-store owners are the segment that can pay (a 5-store owner pays about 34k yen a month against roughly 4.7M yen of food discarded per store per year), that is most exposed to OFC pressure, and that faces the legacy-versus-new-contract expansion decision. One chain means one contract model. Lawson and FamilyMart wait until their subsidy formulas are verified.
mutants.problem: HQ's AI proposes a quantity but never says whose payoff it maximizes. With an 85% owner share of disposal loss, the owner's critical ratio is about 22% (keeps about 24 yen per rice ball sold, loses about 85 yen per one binned) while HQ's is about 70% (earns about 36, loses about 15). Owners cannot audit the proposal and fear the OFC if they deviate. Judges flagged three weaknesses: the asymmetry fades on post-2027 contracts, HQ's markdown push since May 2024 (about 300 items, alerts about 2 hours before expiry) commoditizes a markdown clock, and willingness to pay for software is unproven. Earlier framing as a competing ordering AI also invites a fight with three chains' in-house AI.
mutants.solution: Not a better forecaster, a payoff transform. If HQ's recommended quantity approximates the 70th percentile of demand and the owner's optimum is the 22nd, the owner's cut is about 1.3 standard deviations of the slot's demand spread (about 3.9 units for an item averaging 10 with a spread of 3). The tool therefore needs only the HQ proposal (photo of the order terminal screen or printout), the order actually placed, and the store's hourly sales history to estimate the spread. It returns (1) a ranked Yen Gap sheet: the ten biggest expected-yen differences per delivery slot between HQ's proposal and the owner-optimal quantity under that store's own royalty tier and disposal share; (2) an audit of HQ's markdown clock: for the roughly 300 alerted items and for non-alerted items, whether 'two hours before expiry' is earlier or later than the owner-optimal sticker time given the store's sell-through curve; (3) a neutral 'why I ordered differently' one-pager citing expected value under the owner's contract, shown to the OFC only if the owner chooses; (4) a monthly portfolio page with each store's critical ratio and true hourly wage after royalty and own labor, plus an annual memo on whether the next store should be a legacy expansion or a new-contract store. Nothing touches HQ systems.
mutants.why_now: Osaka's minimum wage rises 54 yen to 1,231 yen on 1 Oct 2026 and Diamond reported a Seven internal simulation with franchisee profit falling to about one third if wages rise on flat sales. HQ AI ordering is now default at all three chains, so owners follow suggestions they cannot audit. Seven's June 2026 announcement of a new contract with a 50% disposal share concedes the point, and creates a two-tier portfolio (legacy versus new stores) that owners have never had to model. Photo OCR of Japanese printouts and cheap LLM-based structuring make a per-owner concierge audit affordable in 2026, which was not true in 2019.
mutants.revenue_model: Entry offer: a paid 30,000 yen '30-day Yen Gap Audit' on one store (credited toward the first 3 months), which tests willingness to pay before any subscription. Then a flat 6,800 yen per store per month (bundle discount at 5+ stores). An annual 150,000 yen next-store-or-renewal decision memo, timed to the moment an owner holds a real 10M-yen decision. Optional 15% gain-share only where a signed baseline exists, so revenue does not depend on disputed savings. Ex-OFC consultants and accountants who refer owners get a 20% revenue share. Bottom-up, if about 5,000 legacy stores sit with 3+ store owners in this segment (an assumption to verify), that is roughly 400M yen a year at full penetration.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The forecast is not the scarce thing, the payoff is. HQ's proposal already encodes a demand distribution, so an owner-side tool can back out the implied quantile and shift it, needing only a spread estimate from the owner's own sales sheets. That makes the product tiny to build and easy to back-test on the founder's three stores. It also flips the political framing: the owner is not overriding HQ's AI, he is applying his own contract to its numbers. Counter-positioning is real, since HQ cannot ship a screen that says its AI is tuned to the wrong payoff without conceding the conflict the JFTC and METI panel already scrutinize.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-7: back-test on the founder's three stores, comparing HQ proposals against realized sales and disposals, estimating the implied quantile and spread per category, and computing the yen gap. Day 3: one-hour paid review by a franchise lawyer of the confidentiality and third-party data clauses. Days 8-20: sell 10 paid 30,000-yen audits through 3-5 ex-OFC consultants, one or two accountants serving multi-store owners, and Kansai owner LINE and Facebook groups. Kill or pivot signal: fewer than 3 paid at 30,000 yen. Days 21-30: deliver audits, convert the willing to 6,800 yen flat with a 60-day money-back guarantee, and publish a one-page legacy-versus-new-contract critical-ratio table (22% versus about 36%) as owner-to-owner content.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Seven, Lawson and FamilyMart AI ordering and Seven's markdown push are treated as the baseline input, not a rival. The product does not compete on forecast accuracy and audits HQ's markdown clock instead of inventing another. Sinops/Sato and Wasteless/Afresh/Shelf Engine sell to retailers and inherit the retailer's payoff, and none uses a franchisee's contract terms. Too Good To Go is an outlet for surplus, not a decision tool. The Okayama union and ex-OFC consultants give advice without calculators, so they become referral partners rather than substitutes, and the channel does not depend on the small Okayama union. Narrowing to legacy Seven stores avoids the per-chain contract complexity and the shrinking-asymmetry problem of post-2027 new stores.

mutants.title: Store Takeover Truth Sheets for Lenders
mutants.one_liner: Buyers and lenders of Japanese convenience-store franchise takeovers pay per deal for an independent contract-aware valuation sheet that shows the store's profit after replacing the owner's own labor, under that store's actual royalty and disposal-share terms, plus the ordering upside a new operator could capture.
mutants.customer: The payer is the acquirer and its lender, not the incumbent owner. First targets are Kansai multi-store franchise corporations buying additional stores, first-time entrants and second-career buyers taking over a store, and the loan officers at regional banks, shinkin banks and Japan Finance Corporation branches financing them, reached through the founder's own lender and succession advisors. The seller supplies the documents because the sale depends on it.
mutants.problem: A store is priced off the HQ-issued statement of 'owner income', which blends profit with wages for unpaid owner and family labor (often 80 to 100 hours a week each) and hides how contract terms bite. At Osaka's 1,231 yen minimum wage, a couple working 140 combined hours a week is worth roughly 9M yen a year before any night premium or manager overhead, so a store showing 10M yen of owner income may earn about 1M yen for a buyer who must hire. A legacy 15/85 disposal contract also hands the buyer 85% of waste risk, while the seller's waste partly reflects HQ-pushed ordering the buyer can change. With Seven's 2027 new contract (50/50, lower charge) never converting existing stores, buyers must now choose between a legacy store and opening a new one on better terms. HQ approves transferees and earns royalties from whoever operates, so it is not a neutral source. Nobody independent computes either adjustment, and this removes the retaliation fear that makes existing owners hard customers.
mutants.solution: An 8-page Store Truth Sheet produced in about 5 business days from seller documents (12 months of HQ monthly statements, disposal totals, hourly sales, labor rosters, the franchise agreement). It shows (1) reported owner income restated as profit after paying market-wage replacement labor at current and scheduled minimum wages, (2) royalty tier and disposal-share mechanics for that specific contract, with sensitivity to wage and sales changes, (3) a range for ordering and markdown upside under the new owner's own payoff (the owner-side newsvendor model), (4) remaining term, transfer and renewal-risk flags, and (5) a legacy versus new-store comparison for buyers who could open a fresh store instead. Lenders get a white-label credit-memo version and a 12-month covenant-monitoring option. Later, buyers who close the deal are the natural first customers for the ordering product.
mutants.why_now: Three shocks landed together: the 1 Oct 2026 wage step in Osaka, Diamond's report of a Seven internal simulation showing franchisee profit falling to about a third under wage increases, and Seven's June 2026 announcement of a 50/50 contract from autumn 2027 for new stores only. That last one splits the market into legacy and new-contract stores and makes the price of a legacy store genuinely uncertain. Extracting numbers from photographed Japanese statements is now cheap, cutting a manual diligence review that would otherwise be a multi-week accountant job. The store-takeover market is assumed to be growing with owner aging, which needs to be verified before scaling.
mutants.revenue_model: 180,000 yen per store diligence sheet paid by the buyer (120,000 yen each when a buyer takes 3 or more stores). Banks that make the sheet a loan condition pay 40,000 yen per file or a per-branch annual license, and can pass it to the borrower. Covenant monitoring at 3,000 yen per store per month for lenders holding loans. Succession advisors who refer deals earn a 10% referral fee. At 10 deals a month this is about 1.8M yen a month, and every sheet adds a contract-parameterized store record to a proprietary benchmark.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The same document set produces two adjustments that point in opposite directions and are both invisible to buyer and seller: owner income falls once labor is priced, and waste upside rises once a new owner uses his own payoff instead of HQ's. Both sides currently negotiate on the HQ statement, so the party with the correct pair of numbers can price a deal better than either side, and a lender will pay for that. Because the buyer pays and has no HQ contract yet, the product sidesteps the fear of OFC retaliation and the franchise-agreement third-party data question is limited to seller-provided records in a sale process. The by-product is a growing cross-store dataset of real royalty, waste and labor economics that nobody outside HQ holds.
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-5: produce Truth Sheets for the founder's own three stores and note the gap between reported income and after-replacement-labor profit. Days 3-10: ask the founder's own lender for a warm introduction to 5 loan officers and reach 3 to 5 succession advisors and multi-store corporations. Publish a free 'profit after replacing yourself' calculator with 6 inputs as the lead magnet. Days 10-30: run 2 free sheets on live deals in exchange for a case study and lender feedback, then sell 3 paid sheets at 180,000 yen (540,000 yen) with a money-back guarantee if the buyer does not find it useful. Kill signal: no live takeover deals found among 15 conversations, in which case the segment volume assumption is false. Also verify seller and HQ data-sharing terms with a franchise lawyer.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: HQ AI ordering and markdown tools (Seven, Lawson, FamilyMart) are operational features with no role in a transaction, and HQ has a conflict as approver and royalty earner. Sinops, Wasteless, Afresh and Shelf Engine sell operations software to retailers and none values a franchise store. Too Good To Go is a surplus outlet. The union and ex-OFC consultants coach owners on markdowns with no calculators and do not sit on the buy side. Sell-side succession and M&A brokers were not covered in the competitor research and need a check, but by design they are paid on completion by the seller. The only independent buy-side underwriting of contract-adjusted owner economics appears unserved.

mutants.title: Franchisee Flight Recorder and Recommendation Index
mutants.one_liner: Invert the advisor into a witness: a silent, tamper-evident ledger that records what the franchisor's AI recommended, what the owner ordered and what was binned, prices the gap under the owner's own contract, and scales into a franchisee-owned registry and a published Recommendation Cost Index for each chain.
mutants.customer: Start with legacy-contract Seven-Eleven owners in Kansai who fear OFC retaliation and will not use a tool that changes how they order. Then a franchisee-owned business cooperative, franchise-specialist law firms, lenders and analysts as data buyers, then regulators and convenience-store review panels as consumers of the aggregate. Later, Lawson and FamilyMart, Korea and Taiwan convenience chains, and other franchise systems with mandated promos, ordering or capex.
mutants.problem: The parent's insight stands: HQ recommendations optimize HQ's payoff. But advice tools stall on the owner's fear of the OFC, on HQ markdown pushes that commoditize the advice, and on Seven's new contract that shrinks the gap for new stores. Meanwhile owners have no evidence in the moments that matter: renewal or non-renewal talks, disputes about mismanagement, store sales, and any complaint to the JFTC or a METI panel. HQ holds the only record of what its AI recommended. The 2009 JFTC order on Seven-Eleven Japan and the Diamond and Toyo Keizai reporting show that regulators and press act on documented owner constraints, but individual owners hold anecdotes and one store is not statistics.
mutants.solution: Owner does nothing differently. Each day a LINE bot takes 3 photos or a forwarded CSV (the HQ order proposal screen, the order as placed, the disposal scan), extracts the data, and writes hashed records to a certified third-party time-stamp so the log is tamper-evident. The owner sees only a private monthly Ledger Statement: 'following HQ's proposals cost you X yen versus the optimum under your contract this month, Y yen cumulative', with no instruction and no OFC-visible change. The ledger is exported only on the owner's command to a lawyer, accountant, buyer or bank. Owners join a franchisee cooperative whose dues also fund a group-rate franchise-law retainer. Aggregated and anonymized across stores, the ledger yields per-item demand models that improve with store count and a quarterly Recommendation Cost Index for each chain, published as a neutral registry that regulators, lenders and press can cite. Every contract change (such as the 2027 Seven terms) becomes a natural experiment the index measures.
mutants.why_now: HQ AI ordering became the default at all three chains between 2023 and 2026, so a recorded 'recommended versus ordered versus binned' history now exists to capture. The disposal-share change in Seven's June 2026 contract shows HQ has conceded the conflict, and the METI convenience-store review panel is active. The 1 Oct 2026 wage step in Osaka makes every wasted yen hurt more. Photo OCR and structured extraction make daily capture cost pennies, and certified time-stamping is standard infrastructure. The outcome of the 2023 union case (loss at the Supreme Court) shows that collective action needs a data and legal structure other than a labor union, which a cooperative can supply.
mutants.revenue_model: 1,980 yen per store per month from owners (about the price of consumer legal-expense insurance, an assumption to verify), with the cooperative dues bundled. Case packs for law firms at 300,000 to 500,000 yen with an expert declaration, optionally a contingency share where the law firm agrees. Annual data licenses to lenders, analysts and research bodies (roughly 3M to 10M yen each). At 15% of about 55,000 stores subscribing that is roughly 200M yen a year from owners alone, before case packs, licenses and other chains or countries. The registry and index are the longer-term standard-setting asset.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The fear that blocks the advice product is the buying reason for the recorder. An owner who will never argue with the OFC will still pay a small fee for a private ledger he never has to show. The value is a network good: one owner's log is an anecdote, but thousands of timestamped logs are the only regulator-grade evidence that a franchisor's recommendations systematically diverge from franchisee payoff, and they cannot be replicated by anyone who lacks owner trust. Because it gives no advice it does not compete with HQ AI on accuracy and is immune to markdown-push commoditization, and it stays useful under any contract terms, including the 50/50 one where a gap remains (owner critical ratio about 36% versus HQ's about 70%).
mutants.first_30_days: Days 1-10: build the LINE bot and ledger on the founder's three stores (the first real evidence file) and commission a one-week franchise-lawyer memo on data ownership and confidentiality plus the business-cooperative structure. Days 10-30: pre-sell 30 owners at 1,980 yen per month for 12 months via Kansai owner LINE and Facebook groups and 2 franchise-focused law firms, pitching it as 'a private record you never have to show anyone unless you need it'. Get one law firm to agree to a case-pack pilot price. Kill signals: fewer than 10 of 30 pre-sales, or the lawyer memo finds the HQ proposal screen cannot be recorded. Publish a one-page description of the Ledger Statement format and the planned index method to seed owner-to-owner sharing.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: It gives no ordering or markdown advice, so it does not compete with Seven, Lawson or FamilyMart AI, with Seven's markdown push, or with Sinops, Wasteless, Afresh and Shelf Engine, all of which are operational tools sold to retailers that inherit the retailer's payoff. Too Good To Go is an outlet for surplus. The union and ex-OFC consultants give advice and community but no evidence base or data, so they become referral channels and cooperative allies. HQ tools are the subject being recorded, and they cannot copy an independent record of their own recommendations without undermining themselves. Power sources: network economies in the pooled index, a cornered resource in owner-contributed logs, switching costs in years of timestamped history.

mutants.title: Paid-But-Dark: Solar Loan Book Audit
mutants.one_liner: A fixed-fee audit and ongoing watch that tells credit unions, servicers and ABS holders which of their solar loans finance a roof that was never switched on. It then cures the worst ones through a supplier-neutral contractor bench.
mutants.customer: Wedge: chief credit or risk officers and loss-mitigation heads at mid-size credit unions and community banks that hold indirect solar loans originated through installer dealer networks. Second wave: servicers and ABS controlling-class investors that inherited books from failed platforms (Solar Servicing LLC-type). Deliberately not the seven Freedom Forever financiers, who already have ops teams and are already staffed. Start with legacy books from Titan, SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, and Mosaic- and Sunlight-financed loans.
mutants.problem: Loan tapes track payments, not power. Many dealer-channel programs released milestone money at 'installed', so a loan on a dark roof looks like ordinary credit stress and gets routed to collections, which is the wrong workout. The holder cannot tell installer-caused non-payment from real credit distress. Reserves are mis-sized and nobody in the institution owns the question 'is the system switched on?'. Judges flagged three weaknesses in the parent: the first wave is already staffed, paperwork-only jobs are price-pressured (Atma quotes up to about $1,200), and demand is lumpy.
mutants.solution: Step 1, a 10-day Book Audit. Ingest the loan tape (address, funding dates, installer ID, milestone dates). Cross-match it to county permit portals, public state interconnection datasets, borrower-authorized monitoring links and installer status. Output a loan-level tier: Energized, Dark-fixable, Dark-blocked-by-records, or Never-started. Add cost-to-cure, expected recovered loan value, and a one-page loss-reserve summary the CFO can hand to auditors. Step 2, a quarterly PTO-lag surveillance subscription on the whole book and on new originations, with installer-health flags, so nothing goes dark silently again. Step 3, cure orchestration at fixed prices by tier, using an open bench (Atma-type installers, Revival, ECG, Optimus, laid-off crews) and engineering subs. GreenLancer can be a supplier here. The paperwork-only tier is passed through at roughly the $1.2k benchmark plus a fixed coordination fee. The margin lives in the audit, the surveillance and the hard tiers (missing hardware, inspection fixes).
mutants.why_now: Freedom Forever went to Chapter 7 on Aug 7, 2026 (claims due Oct 16). It showed that lenders could not see which loans sat on dark roofs, and the same problem is buried in older Titan, SunPower, Sunnova and PosiGen books. The 25D credit ended for 2026 expenditures, so origination volume is down and more installer failures are likely. First-principles cost stack: reading messy permit files and utility portals used to cost $100+ of coordinator time per job. Document and browser agents now do it for a few dollars, so a per-loan audit can be priced below a credit union's discretionary-spend threshold at good margin.
mutants.revenue_model: Audit at $10-20 per loan with a $30k minimum (a 3,000-loan book is about $45-60k). Surveillance at $3-6 per loan per year. Cure coordination fee of $300 on paperwork-only jobs. A 20-30% markup on hard-tier cures ($3-8k each). A $500 PTO bonus. Later, licensing of per-AHJ and per-utility playbooks. Bottom-up: 60 institutions in 24 months at about $60k first-year value is about $3.6M before any cure revenue.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The lender's blind spot is a missing column, not missing crews. Selling to the CFO or CRO's loss-reserve problem, instead of to a loss-mitigation desk waiting for the next bankruptcy, turns event-driven demand into continuous demand. Because the audit is a small fixed-fee purchase and not a vendor selection, it slips under procurement thresholds and creates its own list of jobs to cure. A finding of 'this roof is dark' changes the workout from collections to cure, which is where the loan value is recovered.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: hold 5 calls with credit union CROs and servicer COOs. Ask what they pay today, whether GreenLancer or anyone already covers them, and who owns the reserve question. This is the kill test: if GreenLancer's seven financiers already cover servicers and credit unions, downgrade. Weeks 1-3: build the screen on public data for one state that publishes interconnection records (California's DG Stats is the largest). Publish an anonymized ZIP-level 'permit-final-but-no-PTO' index for Titan and Freedom Forever-era permits as a lead magnet, with no homeowner addresses. Weeks 2-4: offer 3 credit unions a free NDA'd 300-loan scan with a paid full-book option. Recruit 2 ex-installer permit coordinators and sign 2 licensed subs. Goal: one signed paid audit within 60 days.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: GreenLancer sells job-by-job field and engineering work to financiers that already have ops. This sells book-level visibility to holders that have no ops, owns the data layer GreenLancer lacks, and buys GreenLancer-style engineering as a supplier. The seven named lenders and Sunrun/GoodLeap crews keep their in-house step-in, and we do not chase them. We target credit unions, servicers, ABS holders and legacy books. Atma, Revival, ECG and Optimus are the labor bench and not rivals. OhmSnap is homeowner lead-gen and Solar Insure sells warranties to owners after the fact. Enphase's program is post-PTO upsell. None of them sells a lender-side loan-level status product.

mutants.title: Solar Job Escrow: Bankruptcy-Proof Project Records
mutants.one_liner: A neutral escrow that captures every financed solar job's permit, design, serial and step-in authorizations before the installer fails. The installer pays per job, the lender enforces deposits through milestone funding, and cure is paid from the final milestone the lender is still holding.
mutants.customer: Payer: mid-size residential installers (300-3,000 loan-financed jobs a year) that need financing access and a trust signal after Freedom Forever. Gatekeeper and co-seller: dealer-risk and credit heads at solar lenders and credit unions (GoodLeap, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human-type), who can make escrow a dealer-tier condition. Channel: installer CRM, design and project-management platforms that embed the deposit.
mutants.problem: When an installer dies, the permits, interconnection applications, PE-stamped designs, serials and portal logins are locked in the dead company's name, and the lender starts from zero. Every other party (lender, homeowner, trustee) finds out after the fact. Before failure, all of that data exists and is easy to copy. After failure it is expensive to reconstruct. The parent product only starts once the loss has occurred, which is why it is lumpy, price-pressured and crowded.
mutants.solution: Each job auto-deposits a continuity pack at each milestone: signed contract, permit application and approval, PE-stamped design set, interconnection application number, equipment serials by BOM, and time-stamped site photos. Two pre-signed documents go with it. The homeowner signs a successor-contractor authorization as an addendum at the point of sale, and the installer signs a step-in consent. A written trigger (insolvency, license suspension, or 60 days of no activity) releases the pack to a designated successor. The lender's funding portal requires a complete pack before releasing M1 or M2, so deposits cannot be skipped. Trigger jobs are cured at a pre-agreed per-AHJ rate card. The cure is paid from the last milestone (M3) the lender still holds on that job, plus a small installer holdback. Lenders also get a continuity score per dealer (record completeness, PTO lag, license and lien status). Homeowners get a 'job protected' certificate that installers can use in sales.
mutants.why_now: Freedom Forever's collapse made 'will you still be here at PTO?' the first objection at every kitchen table, and made lenders' dealer-risk teams look for controls beyond credit checks. The 25D end is shrinking installer margins and raising failure odds. Agentic capture and CRM APIs make per-job record collection cheap enough for a $60-100 fee. ABS investors can now cite a specific 2026 case when they ask sponsors about continuity.
mutants.revenue_model: Installer pays $60-100 per job (about 0.2-0.3% of a $30-35k job). Lender pays a platform fee of $5-10k a month for dealer continuity scoring and pack access. On a trigger, cure work is billed at $1.5-4k per job plus a $500 PTO bonus, funded from the held M3 milestone. Later: a workmanship warranty backed by the reserve, and a recognized 'backup installer' role in ABS structures. Illustration: 3 pilot installers at 800 jobs each is roughly $145-240k a year in deposit fees before lender fees or cure revenue.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The cure budget already exists. On many dealer-channel loans the final milestone (roughly 10-25% of the loan) is not paid until PTO, so on every stranded job the lender is still holding thousands of dollars that would have gone to the dead installer. The only missing piece is a pre-signed right to spend it. And the escrow has an enforcement mechanism that software-escrow lacked: the lender controls the money, so 'no pack, no milestone payment' means installers deposit because that is how they get paid. The party who needs the protection (the lender) is not the party who pays (the installer), and making escrow a sales badge and a dealer-tier perk closes that gap.
mutants.first_30_days: Draft the continuity pack spec and the successor-contractor authorization with a solar or construction attorney. Map contractor-of-record change rules for the 10 largest AHJs and top 2-3 utilities in one metro. Recruit 5 installers through former installer ops people and offer a free 90-day pilot in exchange for the badge. Call 3 lender dealer-risk heads with a one-page pitch: escrowed dealers get faster funding or lower holdbacks, and you get a first-call cure vendor. Target 3 installer LOIs and 1 lender pilot letter by day 30, and first live deposits by day 60. Riskiest assumption to test: will a lender change its funding conditions for a pilot dealer group. Test it with a credit union first.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: GreenLancer, local rescue contractors and Atma all start after failure, job by job, for an already-staffed lender. This owns the pre-failure moment, sits inside the dealer agreement and the installer's workflow, and earns recurring per-job revenue from installers. When a trigger fires, the company is first-called under a pre-signed rate card and can subcontract to GreenLancer-style shops or local firms. Lender in-house step-in desks have no installer-side records capture, and installers work with 3-5 lenders and will not deposit into five separate lender portals, so neutral multi-lender escrow wins. Solar Insure and OhmSnap serve owners after bankruptcy, and Enphase's program is post-PTO. Main risk is a big lender building a proprietary version, which the neutral multi-lender position is meant to counter.

mutants.title: Dark Roof Capital: Buy, Cure, Re-Perform
mutants.one_liner: Invert the parent. Instead of being paid a $3k fee to cure other people's stranded solar loans, buy those loans at dark-roof prices, finish the systems with a proprietary per-AHJ cure playbook, and keep the full value uplift as a re-performing loan pool.
mutants.customer: Sellers: credit unions, banks, servicers and ABS trusts or controlling-class holders that want dark and forbearance-stuck solar loans off their books. Capital side: distressed-credit funds, family offices and NPL buyers who want a new niche but cannot cure a roof. Homeowners are offered a cure and a payment reset in exchange for reinstating payments.
mutants.problem: Dark solar loans are an orphan asset class with broken pricing. NPL desks discount them to zero collateral value because they cannot fix the system. Lenders will not cure at scale and cannot collect on a roof that produces nothing. A cure costs perhaps 10-15% of the loan balance yet restores most of its value, but a $3k cure fee captures only about 10% of the $20k+ of value created. The holder of the loan keeps 90%, and today nobody who can cure holds the loan.
mutants.solution: Use the forensic pack from the parent as an underwriting engine. Sell a Bid Desk: audit a seller's dark loans, then quote a purchase price within 10 days. First 6 months: sell a zero-upfront cure-share product to a credit union (we finish the jobs, and take about 25% of restored loan value once PTO is achieved and payments resume), funded by a small working-capital line. Then buy pools through an SPV with a licensed sub-servicer. Cure with the playbook and offer borrowers a reset (a rate or principal modification in exchange for reinstatement). Hold or resell re-performing pools. Longer term, securitize re-performing solar loans, as mortgage RPL funds do. Purchases are limited to loans where the borrower is engaged and in forbearance, with reps and warranties and a seller-funded holdback for claims.
mutants.why_now: Freedom Forever, Sunnova, SunPower and PosiGen mean a growing pool of dark loans now exists, with forbearance windows expiring. Post-25D, lenders are shifting from origination to workout and want clean books. Mortgage NPL and RPL buyers already exist and are looking for new asset classes in a higher-rate world. Cheap agentic records recovery makes the per-loan diligence cost low enough to bid on small-balance loans.
mutants.revenue_model: Phase 1 (0-6 months): cure-share, about 25% of restored loan value, with zero upfront cost to the seller. Phase 2: spread on purchased loans. Illustration only: buy a $35k loan at about $11k (roughly 32% of balance), spend about $3.5k to cure, and a re-performing loan is worth about $24-28k, giving a $10-13k gross uplift before servicing, legal and default haircuts. Investors in the SPV pay roughly a 1.5% management fee and 20% carry above an 8% preferred return. The operating company also earns cure and coordination fees. Phase 3: RPL securitization fees.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Fee-for-service captures the wrong slice of value, and whoever can cure at the lowest cost can bid the highest and still make money. Pure NPL funds cannot cure, lenders will not, and cure contractors have no balance sheet, so the buyer with the best per-AHJ playbook has a structural cost advantage. Dark solar loans also carry a specific hidden liability for buyers. Under the FTC Holder Rule, a homeowner can raise installer misconduct claims against whoever holds the loan. Curing the system removes the basis for most of those claims, so the cure is also the de-risking step, and buyers who cannot cure are pricing that risk at its maximum.
mutants.first_30_days: Use the audit engine to build a bid model on 50-100 loans from a friendly credit union or servicer under NDA, and price them. Get a commitment letter from one distressed-credit family office for a $1-2M first-loss pilot. Commission a legal memo on the Holder Rule, state lender and servicer licensing, and rescission risk, and identify a licensed sub-servicer. Sign one cure-share deal (no purchase) covering about 30 loans to measure real cure cost per tier and how many borrowers reinstate. Write a one-page pool teaser for investors. The riskiest assumption is borrower willingness to resume payments and rescission exposure, so measure reinstatement rates before buying anything.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: GreenLancer, Atma, Revival, ECG and Optimus earn service fees and have no balance sheet, and none of them buys loans. The seven Freedom Forever financiers and Sunrun/GoodLeap keep their in-house step-in, but they are holders, not buyers, and they are not the sellers this targets. Credit unions, servicers and trusts that want out are the supply. NPL funds lack cure capability. OhmSnap is homeowner lead-gen, Solar Insure sells owner warranties, and Enphase runs a post-PTO upsell. Revenue comes from loan value uplift, not vendor contracts, so it does not depend on beating GreenLancer for a financier relationship. GreenLancer-style shops and local contractors become subcontractors.

mutants.title: Appraisal Workfile Trustee for Retired and Deceased Appraisers
mutants.one_liner: A neutral custodian that holds a retiring or deceased appraiser's workfiles for 10 years, proves they were never altered, and answers subpoenas, board letters and lender QC requests so the retiree or widow never has to.
mutants.customer: Wedge: sole-proprietor certified residential appraisers aged 62+ who have just gone inactive or announced retirement in 3-4 states (TX, OH, PA, CO), plus heirs and executors of appraisers who die or become incapacitated. These people usually already hold a free LIA or OREP retirement tail, so the money risk is covered and the missing piece is the defense file. Scale payers: E&O administrators and state appraiser associations (loss-control benefit). Requesters (attorneys, lenders, boards) pay production fees where rules allow.
mutants.problem: USPAP requires workfiles to be retained and retrievable for at least 5 years (or 2 years after a judicial proceeding ends), and regulators can act later. A retiree's copy sits on an aging laptop, a USB drive or a software subscription that lapses. The free tail pays defense costs but does not preserve or produce the file, and a workfile with no independent proof of when it was finalized is easy to attack as backfilled. When an appraiser dies, board letters and subpoenas land on a widow with no idea what a workfile is. Nobody answers a subpoena on the retiree's behalf: software vendors store files, they do not act as agent.
mutants.solution: Product v1, 'Seal and Hold': (1) A 60-minute import from a la mode, ClickFORMS or ACI exports or a drive image. Every file is hashed and stamped with a third-party RFC 3161 timestamp, kept in write-once encrypted storage with an index by date, client and address. (2) A custodian agreement naming the Trustee as records custodian and agent for production, plus a notice letter to the state board. (3) A production desk that handles subpoenas, board requests, lender QC and repurchase requests and E&O carrier requests, notifies the retiree or estate, and bills the requester. (4) An estate trigger: named heirs, a death or incapacity switch and pre-filled paperwork. (5) Retention beyond the minimum, with legal-hold extension. Deliberately excluded: trainees, client transfer, earn-outs, tail brokerage.
mutants.why_now: UAD 3.6 becomes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and is pushing veterans to quit rather than relearn. WorkingRE's 2026 survey says 31% plan to leave within 3 years and 57% are over 60, so a predictable wave of exits is starting. Free LIA and OREP tails have made the money side a solved problem, which leaves the file as the remaining exposure. Immutable cold storage and third-party timestamping are commodity-cheap, so intake per retiree is under an hour of ops time.
mutants.revenue_model: $695 one-time for 10-year custody including 3 productions (or $19/month). $995 estate or heir rush plan. Extra productions at $195-450, requester-pays where state rules permit, otherwise billed to the retiree or estate. Group license to E&O administrators and associations at roughly $8-15 per insured per year as loss control (needs validation). Cold storage for about 100 GB costs around $1 per month, so gross margin is 85%+ and the real cost is the production desk and counsel. A two-person team breaks even around 500 custodies a year (assumption).
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The free tail pays the lawyer, but a claim is won or lost on whether the appraiser can produce a file that provably existed in that form on that date. A retiree's own drive cannot prove non-alteration, while a neutral custodian with hash chains and third-party timestamps can. So this is closer to a notary or escrow than to storage, which is why software vendors paid by the user cannot credibly sell it and why insurers, estates and boards have reasons to care. Once the custodian is named in the retiree's board and carrier paperwork, moving away means new attestations, which creates switching costs.
mutants.first_30_days: Week 1: retain counsel for the custodian agreement and a state-by-state memo on retention, board notification, subpoena handling, and confirmation that we are not acting as an appraiser or AMC and no fee-splitting rule applies. Pull public rosters for TX, OH, PA and CO and flag licenses that went inactive or expired in the last 24 months and active licensees licensed 25+ years. Week 2: call 20 of them and pre-sell at $695 with a refund guarantee, then concierge-deliver the first 5 by hand (import 5 years of workfiles, timestamp, issue a custody certificate). Kill rule: fewer than 6 of 20 pay means pivot to insurer-funded only. Week 3: ask LIA and OREP claims managers, two independent E&O agents and one state appraiser association how workfile requests reach them today and whether they would co-brand or fund it as loss control. Meet 3 estate-planning attorneys. Week 4: run a 'What happens to your files when you retire' session through Appraisal Institute chapters and appraiser forums and target 15 paid custodies.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: LIA and OREP sell tail money, not file preservation or production, so they are complements and a possible channel rather than rivals. a la mode/Cotality, ACI and ClickFORMS store files for a paying user but do not act as agent of record, sign attestations or answer subpoenas, and a vendor would take on legal exposure for a lapsed customer, so it is unlikely to respond soon. Aloft, Valligent, Solidifi, AXIS and PAREA are all trainee and supervisor plays, and this idea leaves that lane completely, which also removes the supervisor-of-record burden and trainee-count limits. AppraiseItNow buys only non-residential and specialty practices and offers no custody. Reggora and the AMC consolidators (Class Valuation, Atlas VMS) target lenders and AMC capacity, not individual retirees. Dropping earn-outs, percentage-of-trainee-fees and client transfer removes the fee-splitting, minimum-legal and weak-transferability flaws the research flagged.

mutants.title: Community Lenders Pool Orders to Keep County Appraisers
mutants.one_liner: Sell rural credit unions and banks a pooled, multi-year county 'appraisal continuity compact', where their combined order flow plus a fixed capacity retainer makes a retiring appraiser's territory viable for a supervised successor.
mutants.customer: Payer: the 4-8 community banks and credit unions that originate mortgages in a rural county cluster whose appraiser is retiring, each paying about $3-8k a year, bought through state credit union leagues, bankers associations and their service arms or CUSOs. Beneficiaries: the retiring appraiser (paid a fixed stipend), a mid-career certified appraiser from an adjacent county acting as supervisor, and 1-2 career-changer trainees (agents, inspectors, adjusters).
mutants.problem: A rural lender places 30-100 appraisal orders a year. No single small lender can sustain a trainee, and none is big enough to make an out-of-county appraiser drive 60 miles. When the county's only appraiser retires, orders go to distant AMC panel members, closings slip and purchase loans are lost. Trainee programs like Valligent's assume one lender commits volume. The retiree's book was stable because 15 direct lenders each sent about a dozen orders, so each lender was individually too small to replace it.
mutants.solution: 'County Compact': (1) Diagnose at-risk counties by joining board rosters (active certified appraisers and license age) with HMDA originations by lender and county. (2) Sign a 3-year compact among 4-8 lenders in the county: pooled first-look on local orders (lenders still order directly and independently, with no link to value conclusions or loan approval), a turnaround SLA such as 7 business days, and a fixed annual capacity retainer paid to us. (3) Recruit and equip the continuity team: a certified supervisor plus 1-2 trainees, with desk QC and UAD 3.6 tooling. (4) Pay the retiree a fixed 12-month knowledge-transfer stipend for the recorded local-knowledge interview, adjustment grids, neighborhood boundary notes and lender introductions. The retiree does not sign reports and gets no percentage of anything. (5) Give each lender a quarterly turnaround and quality report for their compliance and board files. Money flow: borrower pays the appraisal fee through the lender at the customary fee, 100% to the appraiser firm with no skim or split. Lenders pay us the retainer. We pay the retiree a fixed stipend and the supervisor a per-trainee capacity stipend. Counsel to confirm the retainer is independent of order outcomes and that we stay under state AMC registration thresholds (roughly 15 appraisers per state, to verify) because lenders order directly.
mutants.why_now: UAD 3.6 goes mandatory Nov 2, 2026 and veterans are choosing to quit. ABA Banking Journal and CSBS have documented rural appraiser shortages in 2026. The AQB exposure draft that drops the college-degree requirement widens the trainee pool. EO 14393 signals regulators want more appraiser supply. State leagues and bankers associations already sell shared services to small members, so the channel exists.
mutants.revenue_model: Capacity retainer of $3-8k per lender per year scaled by originations, so about $30k a year for a 6-lender compact, on 3-year terms. Add-on lender-paid collateral QC or desk review at roughly $45 per report. 10% distribution share to the league or CUSO. Rough economics (assumptions): year 1 costs are about $10k retiree stipend, $10k supervisor and trainee capacity stipends and $5k ops and QC, leaving a thin margin. Years 2-3 drop the retiree stipend, giving about 45-50% gross margin at steady state. 50 compacts is about $1.5M a year.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: Small lenders are each below the minimum viable volume for any successor, but pooled they equal the retiree's book. The compact re-creates that pool contractually. Lenders are not paying for appraisals, which borrowers still cover, but for the option value of local capacity, priced like a rural fire district. A single delayed or lost purchase loan costs a lender more than its share of the retainer, so 2-3 saved closings a year pay for it. Paying supervisors a capacity stipend funded by the pooled retainer solves supervisor scarcity without taking a cut of trainee fees, so fee-splitting rules are avoided.
mutants.first_30_days: Build a county risk map for TX, OH, PA and CO from board rosters and HMDA and NCUA/FFIEC lender lists, and shortlist 15 counties with an aging appraiser and 4+ community lenders. Call appraisal or ordering managers at 20 credit unions and banks and ask which orders were delayed or unplaceable in the last 12 months and what each cost. Offer two state leagues or bankers associations free county risk maps for their members as the door-opener and ask for a pilot. Recruit 2 supervisors and 4 trainees. Get a signed letter of intent for 2 pilot compacts of 3+ lenders each. Commission one counsel memo on appraisal independence and AMC thresholds.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Valligent is national, hires supervisors as employees and relies on a single lender's volume commitment, with no retiree knowledge handoff. This is a county-pooled, multi-lender contract with fixed stipends and no employment. Aloft is a centralized company-appraiser model, not local continuity. Solidifi and AXIS are AMC mentor-matching programs, while this is lender-funded capacity in named counties. PAREA gives experience without supervisors but transfers no local knowledge and does not guarantee anyone orders. Reggora and the AMC consolidators (Class Valuation, Atlas VMS) are platforms and cannot easily offer a multi-lender contractual pool for one county. LIA, OREP and a la mode do not touch this. Fixed stipends and no percentage of trainee or successor revenue avoid the fee-splitting and earn-out legality problems, and the retiree does not need to stay licensed.

mutants.title: Rural Sales Commons: Pay Retiring Appraisers for Comps
mutants.one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of retirees paying to leave, pay them for their verified sales books and build the private sales-price registry that non-disclosure states lack, sold first to practicing rural appraisers and later to AVM, lender and assessor buyers.
mutants.customer: Supply (paid): retiring and retired certified residential appraisers in roughly a dozen non-disclosure states (for example TX, UT, ID, MT, WY, NM, KS, LA, MS, ND), starting with Texas.
