Demand: practicing rural appraisers first (subscription), then AVM and hybrid-valuation vendors, rural lenders' collateral-risk teams, county assessors for ratio studies, and eventually programs expanding alternative valuations.
mutants.problem: In non-disclosure states, sale prices are not in public deed records. For non-MLS rural sales (FSBO, family transfers, auctions, seller-financed land-with-house), the only record of price is often an appraiser's own phone-confirmation notes and comp files. When the appraiser retires, that sales book is thrown out or dies on a hard drive. Practicing appraisers then struggle to find defensible comps, AVMs and desktop valuations are weakest exactly there (hypothesis to test), and human appraisers stay indispensable and scarce.
mutants.solution: Wedge product: a 'Rural Comp Finder' subscription for practicing appraisers in one region, built from a paid capture program. (1) Sales Book Capture: a 2-day white-glove engagement in which we ingest the retiree's comp libraries (a la mode or ClickFORMS exports, spreadsheets, paper binders) with LLM parsing. We keep only transaction facts (date, price, terms, property characteristics, verification source and method), plus the retiree's own adjustment grids and market-area notes. Client and borrower identities never enter the system, and MLS-derived fields are tagged and excluded. The retiree signs a license and certifies what is theirs. (2) Product: county-level search showing each verified sale with provenance (who confirmed, how, when) and a confidence grade, plus a paired-sales adjustment library. (3) Contributor loop: active appraisers who add confirmed sales get a discount, so the commons refreshes after the retirees are gone. (4) Later products: API and data licenses to AVM and hybrid vendors, lenders and county assessors, positioned as ground truth for validating AVMs and alternative valuations.
mutants.why_now: About 6-7k appraisers a year are expected to leave (31% of a roughly 65k workforce within 3 years per WorkingRE), and each exit destroys a sales book permanently. UAD 3.6 (mandatory Nov 2, 2026) pushes the industry toward structured data. EO 14393 expands alternative valuations, which need ground truth in thin markets. LLM extraction of messy comp files (old exports, PDFs, handwritten binders) became cheap enough in 2025-26 to make capture affordable.
mutants.revenue_model: Subscriptions of $39-59 per month per region for active appraisers (contributors pay less). Data licenses of about $25-120k per state per year to AVM and hybrid vendors and lenders, and $15-40k per year to assessors (all unvalidated). Retirees are paid $1,500-3,000 upfront plus a 20-25% royalty pool shared by verified contribution, and that payout is our main cost of goods. Rough plan (assumptions): 20 retirees x about $2,000 is $40k to acquire perhaps 50-100k verified records. 300 subscribers by month 12 is roughly $210k ARR before any data licenses.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The parent asks retirees to pay, but a retiree is a supplier with a ticking clock. Each exit permanently deletes an asset that no later entrant can recreate, and scraping cannot reach it because the value is provenance: who confirmed this price, how and when. First to sign the last generation of phone-confirming appraisers cornered a resource competitors cannot buy once it is gone. Practicing appraisers contributing new confirmed sales gives the commons a network effect that outlasts the retirees. The moat is the counsel-designed data model (provenance tagging, MLS exclusion, client stripping), which turns legal risk into a barrier to fast followers. Because retirees are paid, the parent's unproven willingness-to-pay problem disappears and no earn-out or client transfer is needed.
mutants.first_30_days: Gating step: a counsel memo on MLS license terms, the USPAP Confidentiality Rule, GLBA and state board views, and stop or redesign if the extractable data set is too thin. Interview 15 retirees and 15 active appraisers in Texas and ask to see their comp books. Buy 5 sales books at $1,500 as paid pilots, parse them with an LLM pipeline, and tag provenance and MLS-derived rows. Run a blind coverage test on one rural county: how many verified non-MLS sales in the last 5 years the commons holds versus what an active appraiser or an AVM can find. Show the test to 3 AVM or hybrid-valuation vendors and 3 rural lenders and ask for letters of intent. Pre-sell a $39 per month beta to 30 active appraisers. Because the web-search budget ran out, also verify in week 1 whether Cotality, ATTOM or any appraiser comp-sharing group already sells verified non-MLS sales in non-disclosure states.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: None of the parent's competitors sell data: LIA and OREP sell tail coverage, a la mode stores each user's own files, and Aloft, Valligent, Solidifi, AXIS and PAREA are trainee and supervisor programs, so this idea leaves the trainee, supervisor and client-handoff lane entirely. Aloft, Reggora and AMC-side firms are more likely buyers of the data than competitors. Incumbent data vendors (Cotality, ATTOM, MLS aggregators) depend on MLS feeds and recorder data and would have to buy retiree confirmations one appraiser at a time, which does not fit their scale (unverified, to check in week 1). The design avoids fee-splitting law because no appraisal fee or client revenue is shared, avoids supervisor-licensing issues, and avoids weak client transferability because no clients move.

mutants.title: Nonrenewal Desk for Colorado Independent Agencies
mutants.one_liner: An agent-side triage-and-evidence service that starts when a Front Range nonrenewal or score-disclosure notice lands, and charges most of its fee only when the policy is saved.
mutants.customer: Owner-principals of independent insurance agencies in Boulder, Jefferson, Larimer, El Paso and Douglas counties. Each has 150+ wildland-urban-interface homeowner policies, is appointed with 6 or more carriers so it can re-market, and has received several nonrenewals or surcharge notices since January 2026. Colorado only. California is dropped until AB 75 is confirmed enacted.
mutants.problem: When a nonrenewal or score disclosure arrives, the agent has about 10 days to get an acknowledgement and about 30 days to a decision (HB25-1182). The agent has no verified evidence, and the free homeowner kits (FireRisk.ai, Defensible Space Score) only produce letters. A corrected score may not move the premium, because insurers can meet the law with a manual mitigation discount and do not have to accept third-party imagery. The agent loses the commission and the bundled auto and umbrella policies, roughly $600 a year or more per WUI household.
mutants.solution: The agent forwards the notice PDF and gets three things within 48 hours. (1) A Lot Ledger: dated 15-50 cm imagery and public lidar canopy and clearance measurements set against each feature the insurer disclosed. Each feature is marked contradicted, confirmed or unknowable. (2) A Credit Map: for each carrier the agency is appointed with, which filed mitigation credits or underwriting-exception paths the evidence supports, so the pack asks for the premium or retention outcome and not just a score change. (3) A carrier-formatted pack timed to the 10 and 30 day clocks, plus a re-marketing shortlist when the appeal is weak. The desk declines to file when the evidence does not contradict the score. That keeps the concession ledger clean and makes carriers trust the packs. After trust is built, the same imagery layer is run across the agency's whole WUI book to flag likely errors before renewal.
mutants.why_now: HB25-1182 has been in force since July 1, 2026, so disclosures, appeals and the 10/30-day clocks are now real for every Colorado WUI policy. Independent agents are the ones absorbing the nonrenewals. Public regional aerial flights, USGS-style lidar and cheap commercial archives mean the first appeals need no imagery licence. I did not verify that insurer appeal desks are unprepared, so the plan does not rely on it; the trigger is the notice itself.
mutants.revenue_model: $249 per month per agency, including 5 triage runs and a book scan of up to 300 WUI policies. Extra packs are $149 each. A flat $300 success fee applies per policy retained or re-marketed within 90 days of a pack. There is no percentage of premium, to avoid producer-compensation and rebating problems. At 20 agencies, that is about $60k in subscriptions plus roughly $90k in success fees, around $150k ARR, with gross margin above 70% once imagery is bought per filed case only.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The product is a decision about what will actually change the outcome: fix the input, harden the house, or re-market it. It is not a rebuttal letter. Honest triage is the moat, because a desk that refuses weak cases gets a higher concession rate, and a concession ledger keyed by carrier, vendor, input error and evidence type becomes something carriers cannot get elsewhere. Carrier-side vendors like Zesty, Nearmap and Cotality cannot sell against their own customers' scores. That is counter-positioning.
mutants.first_30_days: Recruit 6 Front Range agencies through a Colorado independent-agent association or by direct outreach to principals. Run concierge delivery by hand with an analyst using public imagery, lidar and QGIS, with no licensing. Give the first 5 files per agency free and charge $99 from file 6. Aim for 40 real notices and 20 filed appeals with outcomes tracked. Send agencies a private weekly concession scoreboard as the sales asset.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: FireRisk.ai and DefensibleHome sell homeowner letters and templates with no imagery and no verification. This sells verified evidence and a decision to agents, who buy per book and not per household. The Defensible Space Score is free and self-reported, and the desk is what an agent uses when self-reports fail. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home and Wildfire Partners are slow on-site certifications, and they become a channel later. Road Home Exteriors bundles packets with hardening jobs and does not scan books or work the clocks. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk are carrier-side and conflicted, and the desk does not compete with their scoring. The risk that one of them bolts on a policyholder module is met by locking in agency distribution and the concession ledger early, and by considering a data partnership with one of them.

mutants.title: Insurable-at-Closing: Pay-on-Closing Insurability Sheets for WUI Listings
mutants.one_liner: Listing agents order a 48-hour parcel evidence and carrier-routing sheet before a wildfire-zone home goes to market, and the seller pays a flat fee at closing only if the sale closes.
mutants.customer: Listing agents and brokerages selling wildland-urban-interface homes in Front Range and mountain markets such as the Boulder foothills, Evergreen and Conifer, Estes Park, Black Forest and the Colorado Springs foothills. Title and escrow officers are the channel, and the seller pays through the settlement statement. A licensed WUI-specialist independent agency is the placement partner.
mutants.problem: A lender will not close without a bound homeowners policy. In WUI sales the bind often fails late: the buyer's quote is declined on a score cutoff and the contract clock is running. Neither the seller's nor the buyer's agent can say in advance which carriers will write the lot. No statute helps at that point, because the new-business decline is not a nonrenewal appeal. Free homeowner appeal kits do not touch this moment.
mutants.solution: When the home is listed, the agent orders an Insurability Sheet. It is a one-page PDF and a data file with a lot condition ledger from dated imagery and lidar, a ranked list of pre-closing fixes with cost and time to complete, and a carrier route showing which carriers' models see this lot accurately and have a human exception path. The partner agency supplies indicative appetite and quotes. At contract, buyers' agents can re-run the sheet in 24 hours. The lot evidence goes to underwriters as an exception referral at carriers that read it, and away from carriers using coarse 30 m models that will decline the same lot on a raster.
mutants.why_now: Colorado WUI homeowners' rates roughly doubled in 2020-2025 (per the parent research) and carriers keep retreating, so insurance availability is now a closing risk. HB25-1182 disclosures mean sellers can now hold a score but not a plan. Cheap high-resolution archives make a 48-hour turnaround affordable. I could not verify local closing-fall-through statistics or new pre-listing tools in this pass, so check both first.
mutants.revenue_model: A $395 flat fee on the settlement statement, due only if the sale closes; $150 upfront if the agent prefers. A $75 rapid re-run for buyer-side agents. A placement technology fee or revenue share from the partner agency on policies bound (about 10-15% commission on roughly $5k premiums, renewing yearly), structured with counsel around RESPA and producer-compensation rules. At 8% of roughly 6,000 annual WUI sales in the five focus counties, that is about $0.2M in fees in year one. Expanding across the Western WUI markets lifts this to the low tens of millions.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The same lot gets very different treatment from different carriers. The parent research cites identical Class A homes receiving discounts of 0.7%, 12% and 41%. That suggests the profitable move is routing the lot to the carrier whose model sees it correctly, and not rebutting a score. Routing needs no statutory appeal right, so it works in California, Oregon and Washington where the Colorado law does not apply. The moat is a bindability database of carrier appetite by parcel features and actual bind outcomes. Score vendors see scores, not who binds, and agents see only their own quotes.
mutants.first_30_days: Sign one Front Range WUI-specialist independent agency as the licensed placement partner. Recruit 2 title or escrow offices and 5 listing agents. Run 20 listings with the fee contingent on closing and track policy-bound-before-closing rate, days saved and deals rescued. Get a written RESPA and producer-compensation review before any fee reaches a bank account. Turn the results into one case study for brokerage sales meetings.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome and the Defensible Space Score serve homeowners disputing an existing score and have nothing for the sale moment or for carrier routing. IBHS and Wildfire Partners are on-site programs that take weeks, and they do not fit a 30-day contract, though they could later validate a sheet. Road Home Exteriors sells evidence with hardening jobs, not before a sale. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk score for carriers and do not see the buyer's bind attempt. Possible new rivals are quote-at-offer tools and portals with climate scores; they quote from their own models with no lot evidence and no multi-carrier routing. I could not check for those in this pass.

mutants.title: Notarized Mitigation Records: The Evidence Standard for Wildfire Credits
mutants.one_liner: A score-agnostic verification layer where contractors capture signed photos that are cross-checked against imagery and issued as portable machine-readable Verified Mitigation Records, which carriers and certifiers accept.
mutants.customer: First, Front Range defensible-space crews, roofers, ember-vent installers and drone inspectors, who pay per job. Then wildfire certification programs (Wildfire Partners, IBHS-style programs) that pay per avoided inspection. Then carriers' appeal desks and underwriters, who read the record through a free API and later pay for ingestion. HOAs and fire-safe councils are the bulk channel.
mutants.problem: Homeowners spend $5k-$30k hardening a house and cannot prove it in a way an insurer will accept. Photos and photo-log templates are easy to fake, and AI image generation makes unverified photos worth less each year. HB25-1182 obliges insurers to credit documented mitigation but sets no evidence standard, and on-site inspection capacity is the bottleneck. Contractors cannot promise an insurance credit, so hardening jobs stay unsold.
mutants.solution: A web app (PWA first) for contractors and homeowners with guided capture: a checklist of shots for Zone 0/1/2, vents, roof and gutters, taken with signed capture (C2PA-style content credentials, device attestation, GPS, time and heading). The system cross-checks each claim against archived and new imagery and lidar, for example that vegetation was cleared between two dated images or that a roof is Class A. It issues a Verified Mitigation Record as an open-schema JSON file plus a PDF, versioned and portable across carriers. The schema is published under an open licence and co-developed with a fire-safe council. Carrier and certifier readers are free, and acceptance outcomes feed a per-carrier acceptance dataset. The capture layer would use an existing signed-capture SDK, not a new one.
mutants.why_now: Generative image tools have made unverified photo evidence untrustworthy. Signed-capture standards and SDKs are now commodity. HB25-1182 turned documented mitigation into a legal object with no format. High-resolution archives and public lidar are cheap enough to act as the independent witness. This is also the inversion of the parent idea: instead of proving a model wrong about the house, prove the house right and let any score-maker read it.
mutants.revenue_model: $49-$89 per notarized job, paid by the contractor and passed through in the quote. $40-$120 per avoided on-site reinspection from certification programs. $15-$60 per accepted record from carriers via subscription or API. Agents from a rebuttal desk buy per file. At 300 contractors doing 40 records a year at $65, that is about $0.8M, and the carrier and certifier layers scale it much further.
mutants.non_obvious_insight: The reason insurers can decline third-party imagery is that they cannot trust or parse it, not that they are hostile. Give them evidence with provenance, in a schema they can auto-ingest, and the cost of handling an appeal falls. The parent's moat, the concession database, then extends into a network: contractors, homeowners and carriers all gain from a shared format, as with ACORD forms or the Uniform Appraisal Dataset. Because the layer describes the house and not the score, it holds up when Zesty, Cotality or Verisk change their models, and it is neutral in a way a scorer can never be.
mutants.first_30_days: Sign 5 Boulder and Jefferson County defensible-space and roofing contractors on a free pilot. Ship the guided-capture PWA with the imagery cross-check. Notarize 60 real jobs. Ask 3 agencies to submit those records in real credit requests and log carrier responses. Propose a 10-file remote pre-verification pilot to Wildfire Partners. Publish schema v0.1 on GitHub.
mutants.how_it_avoids_competitors: Road Home Exteriors and other contractors packaging evidence are customers and distribution, not rivals; this gives their packets carrier-grade credibility. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home and Wildfire Partners are channel partners, because remote pre-verification cuts their on-site cost. FireRisk.ai, DefensibleHome and the Defensible Space Score offer letters and unverifiable photo-log templates, which the record replaces. Zesty, Nearmap, Cape, Cotality and Verisk are scorers that would consume the record and cannot be the neutral notary because they are the party being rebutted. The real risks are a signed-capture vendor such as Truepic moving into wildfire, and a scorer building its own format. The defences are the wildfire-specific schema, the per-carrier acceptance data, and being paid by contractors for jobs.
